intro: These endings all turn a plain statement into a comment about it. のだ / んです presents a fact as the explanation behind a situation; わけ states what follows logically from facts; もの speaks about the nature of things, social norms and fond memories; こと gives advice, says something is unnecessary, or reports and rephrases. One neighbour joins them in the mixed set: はず, the speaker's expectation about a single case. Before you choose, ask whether you are explaining, concluding, generalising, advising or predicting.

skills.rule: Add んです (written のです, casual んだ / の) when you explain a situation or ask about the story behind one; leave it off for bare facts with nothing to explain.
skills.explain:
〜んです ties what you say to a situation both speakers can see or already know. It means 'the thing is...' or 'you see'. 頭が痛いんです answers the unspoken question 'why do you look ill?'. In questions it asks for the background to something you have noticed: どうしたんですか ('what happened?'), 日本語が上手ですね。どこで勉強したんですか.

Form: plain form + んです. Nouns and na-adjectives take な: 学生なんです, 静かなんです. Past: 行ったんです, 休みだったんです. Formal writing uses のです / のだ; casual speech uses んだ, or の in questions and soft statements.

Use it for reasons, excuses, surprise, and as a lead-in to a request (〜たいんですが、…). Do not use it for neutral information with no situation behind it, such as a self-introduction or a timetable: 田中です, not 田中なんです. Used everywhere, it sounds insistent or emotional.
patterns: [plain form] んです / のです
どうして / どこで … んですか

examples.jp: どうした{んですか}。
examples.en: What's the matter?

examples.jp: 来週[らいしゅう]、引[ひ]っ越[こ]す{んです}。
examples.en: The thing is, I'm moving next week.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は休[やす]みな{んです}か。
examples.en: Oh, so you're off tomorrow?

examples.jp: すみません、道[みち]が混[こ]んでいた{んです}。
examples.en: Sorry, the roads were jammed (that's why I'm late).

examples.jp: 駅[えき]へ行[い]きたい{んです}が、道[みち]を教[おし]えていただけませんか。
examples.en: I'd like to get to the station. Could you tell me the way?

contrast.note: です simply states. 雨です = it's raining (a report). 雨なんです = it's raining, you see (and that is why...). Use plain です when nothing needs explaining.
でしょう guesses; んです presents the explanation as known. 疲れているんでしょう = you must be tired (my guess at the reason); 疲れているんです = I'm tired (that's the reason).
そうです passes on hearsay: 休みだそうです = I hear it's a holiday. 休みなんです asserts it yourself, as the explanation.

mistakes.bad: 初[はじ]めまして。田中[たなか]{なんです}。
mistakes.good: 初[はじ]めまして。田中[たなか]{です}。
mistakes.note: A self-introduction explains nothing; んです makes it sound like an excuse or a reply to doubt.

mistakes.bad: 明日[あした]は休[やす]み{んです}。
mistakes.good: 明日[あした]は休[やす]みな{んです}。
mistakes.note: Nouns and na-adjectives need な before んです.

skills.tip: Is there an unspoken 'why?' or 'you see' in the air? Then んです; if not, plain です.

skills.rule: わけだ = 'so that's why / no wonder'; わけがない = 'there's no way'; わけではない = 'it's not (necessarily) that'; わけにはいかない = 'I can't, because it wouldn't be right'.
skills.explain:
わけ means 'reason, logic'. Each pattern says what follows, or does not follow, from the facts.

わけだ draws the conclusion the facts lead to: 十年も住んでいたから、上手なわけだ ('so no wonder she's good'). 道理で…わけだ is the set 'no wonder' phrase.

わけがない (casual わけない) rules a possibility out completely: あの人が嘘をつくわけがない ('there's no way he'd lie').

わけではない denies only part of a statement or an assumption, and softens it: 嫌いなわけではない ('it's not that I dislike it'). It often comes with いつも, 全部, 必ずしも.

わけにはいかない says you cannot do something for social or moral reasons, not physical ones: 約束したから、行かないわけにはいかない ('I promised, so I can't not go'). For lack of ability, use the potential form or できない.

All four follow the plain form; na-adjectives take な (好きなわけ), and nouns usually take という (学生というわけではない).
patterns: [plain form] わけだ (道理で … わけだ)
[plain form] わけではない / というわけではない
[dictionary form / ない-form] わけにはいかない

examples.jp: 毎日[まいにち]練習[れんしゅう]しているから、上手[じょうず]な{わけだ}。
examples.en: She practises every day, so no wonder she's good.

examples.jp: 窓[まど]が開[あ]いている。道理[どうり]で寒[さむ]い{わけだ}。
examples.en: The window's open. No wonder it's cold.

examples.jp: こんなに難[むずか]しい問題[もんだい]が、子供[こども]に解[と]ける{わけがない}。
examples.en: There's no way a child could solve a problem this hard.

examples.jp: 高[たか]い服[ふく]がいつもいい{わけではない}。
examples.en: Expensive clothes aren't always good.

examples.jp: 肉[にく]が嫌[きら]いな{わけではありません}。今日[きょう]は食[た]べたくないだけです。
examples.en: It's not that I dislike meat. I just don't want any today.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は試験[しけん]だから、休[やす]む{わけにはいかない}。
examples.en: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.

contrast.vs: わけではない / わけがない
contrast.note: わけではない denies part ('it's not that...'); わけがない denies all ('no way'). 高いわけではない = it isn't exactly expensive; 高いわけがない = it can't possibly be expensive.
できない / the potential form is about ability or circumstance; わけにはいかない means 'I could, but I mustn't'. お金がないから買えない (no money) against 人のお金だから使うわけにはいかない (it isn't mine to spend).
はずがない and わけがない are near-equals when denying outright; はずがない leans on expectation, わけがない on logic.

mistakes.bad: この漢字[かんじ]は難[むずか]しくて、読[よ]む{わけにはいかない}。
mistakes.good: この漢字[かんじ]は難[むずか]しくて、{読[よ]めない}。
mistakes.note: Not knowing the kanji is a lack of ability, so use the potential form; わけにはいかない is for social or moral barriers.

mistakes.bad: 彼[かれ]は優[やさ]しい人[ひと]だから、そんなことを言[い]う{わけではない}。
mistakes.good: 彼[かれ]は優[やさ]しい人[ひと]だから、そんなことを言[い]う{わけがない}。
mistakes.note: To rule something out completely, use わけがない; わけではない is only a partial denial.

skills.tip: だ concludes, がない rules out, ではない softens, にはいかない refuses on principle.

skills.rule: ものだ states how things naturally are or how people should behave (with the た-form: 'used to', fondly); ものではない says 'one shouldn't'; ものだから / もん gives a personal excuse.
skills.explain:
もの is 'thing': ものだ talks about the nature of things, not about one event.

General truth: 人は変わるものだ ('people change; that's how people are'), 時間が経つのは早いものだ.

Social norm: 年上の人には敬語を使うものだ ('one uses keigo to older people'). The negative ものではない means 'one shouldn't' and is typical when scolding: 人の悪口を言うものではない.

Nostalgia: た-form + ものだ = 'used to', for repeated habits in a time now gone: 昔はよくこの川で泳いだものだ. It cannot describe an ordinary single event; with one event it only appears in exclamations such as よく頑張ったものだ.

Strong wish: 一度行ってみたいものだ ('I'd really love to go some time').

As a reason, ものだから / もので ('because, you see') offers an excuse, usually for something that went wrong. Sentence-final もの / もん after a plain form (だって眠いんだもん) is casual and sounds young or pleading.
patterns: [dictionary form] ものではない (one shouldn't)
[plain form] ものだから / もので / もん (excuse)

examples.jp: 子供[こども]はよく転[ころ]ぶ{ものだ}。
examples.en: Children fall over a lot; that's what they're like.

examples.jp: 時間[じかん]が経[た]つのは早[はや]い{ものです}ね。
examples.en: Time really does fly, doesn't it.

examples.jp: 食[た]べながら話[はな]す{ものではない}。
examples.en: You shouldn't talk while you're eating.

examples.jp: 若[わか]いころは、よく夜遅[よるおそ]くまで遊[あそ]んだ{ものだ}。
examples.en: When I was young, I often used to stay out late.

examples.jp: 道[みち]が混[こ]んでいた{ものですから}、遅[おく]れてしまいました。
examples.en: The roads were jammed, you see, so I was late.

examples.jp: だって、知[し]らなかったんだ{もん}。
examples.en: But I didn't know!

contrast.note: ことだ advises one listener in one situation ('the thing for you to do is'); ものだ states the norm for everyone. 早く寝ることだ = you should get to bed early; 子供は早く寝るものだ = children ought to go to bed early.
わけだ concludes from the facts in front of you ('so that's why'); ものだ states what is true in general, whatever this case is.
はずだ is an expectation about one case (彼はもう家にいるはずだ, 'he should be home by now'); ものだ is a general truth.

mistakes.bad: 昨日[きのう]、海[うみ]で泳[およ]いだ{ものだ}。
mistakes.good: 子供[こども]のころ、毎年[まいとし]海[うみ]で泳[およ]いだ{ものだ}。
mistakes.note: Nostalgic たものだ needs a repeated habit from a time now past, not a single recent event.

skills.tip: Could you add 'that's just how it is' or 'that's what people do'? Then ものだ.

skills.rule: ことだ = 'the best thing for you to do is'; ことはない = 'there's no need to'; ということだ = 'I hear that' or 'that means'.
skills.explain:
こと is an abstract 'matter'; these patterns point to the one thing that counts.

ことだ gives direct advice to someone in a particular situation: 上手になりたければ、毎日練習することだ ('if you want to improve, practise every day'). The negative advice is ないことだ: 無理をしないことだ. It is firm and comes from above (teacher, parent, senior), so do not use it to a superior.

ことはない says there is no need: 心配することはない ('there's no need to worry'). It reassures someone who is about to do more than necessary. It is never a prohibition; 'must not' is てはいけない.

ということだ has two uses. Hearsay, rather formal, like そうだ: 来週は休みだということだ ('I hear next week is off'). Conclusion or rephrasing, often with つまり: つまり、明日は無理だということですね ('so that means tomorrow is out').

examples.jp: そんなに心配[しんぱい]する{ことはない}よ。
examples.en: There's no need to worry so much.

examples.jp: 風邪[かぜ]を早[はや]く治[なお]したいなら、ゆっくり休[やす]む{ことだ}。
examples.en: If you want to get over your cold quickly, the thing to do is rest.

examples.jp: わざわざ来[く]る{ことはありません}。電話[でんわ]で大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です。
examples.en: There's no need to come all this way. A phone call is fine.

examples.jp: 天気予報[てんきよほう]によると、明日[あした]は雪[ゆき]が降[ふ]る{ということだ}。
examples.en: According to the forecast, it's going to snow tomorrow.

examples.jp: 返事[へんじ]がないのは、来[こ]ない{ということです}ね。
examples.en: No reply means they aren't coming, then.

contrast.note: ものだ is the general norm for everyone; ことだ is advice to you, now.
Both mean 'no need', but ことはない always adds 'don't bother / don't worry' to someone about to overdo it; なくてもいい is neutral permission not to.
ということだ reports or rephrases ('I hear' / 'that means'); わけだ explains something you have noticed ('no wonder'). 会議は中止だということだ = I hear the meeting is off; 会議が中止だから静かなわけだ = no wonder it's quiet.

mistakes.bad: 危[あぶ]ないから、ここで遊[あそ]ぶ{ことはない}。
mistakes.good: 危[あぶ]ないから、ここで遊[あそ]ん{ではいけない}。
mistakes.note: ことはない means 'no need to', not 'don't'; a prohibition needs てはいけない.

mistakes.bad: 部長[ぶちょう]、今日[きょう]は早[はや]く帰[かえ]って休[やす]む{ことです}。
mistakes.good: 部長[ぶちょう]、今日[きょう]は早[はや]めにお帰[かえ]りになっ{てはいかがですか}。
mistakes.note: ことだ is advice from above; to a superior, make a polite suggestion instead.

skills.tip: Advice to you: ことだ. 'Don't bother': ことはない. 'So I hear / so that means': ということだ.

skills.rule: Ask in order: advice or hearsay (こと)? true in general or a fond habit (もの)? an expectation about one case (はず)? the explanation of a known fact (わけ)?
skills.explain:
Run these questions in order and stop at the first yes.

1. Am I advising this listener, saying there is no need, or reporting what I heard? → ことだ, ことはない, ということだ.
2. Am I stating how things are in general, what people ought to do, or a habit I remember fondly? → ものだ, ものではない, たものだ.
3. Am I predicting one particular case from what I know, something not yet confirmed? → はずだ ('should be'), はずがない ('can't be').
4. Am I explaining a fact that is already in front of me? → わけだ ('no wonder'). Partial denial: わけではない. Refusal on principle: わけにはいかない.

The hard border is はず against わけ. Only はず predicts: 鍵を渡したから入れるはずだ. Only わけ does the other わけ jobs (partial denial, refusal). They overlap in two places: when you discover the reason for a fact (道理で寒いはず / わけだ, both 'no wonder'), and in outright denial (はずがない, わけがない).
patterns: ことだ — the thing for you to do is
ものだ — that's how things are / one should
はずだ — it should be (I expect)

examples.jp: 子供[こども]は外[そと]で元気[げんき]に遊[あそ]ぶ{ものだ}。
examples.en: Children are meant to play outside and be lively.

examples.jp: 元気[げんき]になりたいなら、外[そと]で体[からだ]を動[うご]かす{ことだ}。
examples.en: If you want to get healthy, the thing to do is get moving outdoors.

examples.jp: 鍵[かぎ]を渡[わた]したから、もう家[いえ]に入[はい]れる{はずだ}。
examples.en: I gave him the key, so he should be able to get in now.

examples.jp: 鍵[かぎ]を持[も]っていなかったのか。それで入[はい]れなかった{わけだ}。
examples.en: He didn't have the key? So that's why he couldn't get in.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんは三年[さんねん]フランスにいたから、フランス語[ご]が話[はな]せる{はずだ}。
examples.en: Ms Tanaka lived in France for three years, so she should be able to speak French.

examples.jp: 三年[さんねん]もフランスにいたんですか。それでフランス語[ご]が上手[じょうず]な{わけですね}。
examples.en: You lived in France for three years? So that's why your French is so good.

contrast.note: Is the result confirmed? Not yet: はず (a forecast). Yes, and you are giving its reason: わけ.
True for everyone, always: もの. Advice to this person, now: こと.

contrast.vs: わけではない / はずがない
contrast.note: わけではない only softens ('it's not that...'); はずがない rules out completely ('it can't be').

mistakes.bad: 田中[たなか]さんはまだ来[き]ていないけど、もうすぐ着[つ]く{わけだ}。
mistakes.good: 田中[たなか]さんはまだ来[き]ていないけど、もうすぐ着[つ]く{はずだ}。
mistakes.note: A forecast about something not yet confirmed needs はず; わけだ explains a fact you already have.

mistakes.bad: 風邪[かぜ]を引[ひ]いたなら、薬[くすり]を飲[の]んで寝[ね]る{わけだ}。
mistakes.good: 風邪[かぜ]を引[ひ]いたなら、薬[くすり]を飲[の]んで寝[ね]る{ことだ}。
mistakes.note: Advice to the listener is ことだ; わけだ never advises.

skills.tip: Advice to you: こと. True of everyone: もの. Expected, not yet confirmed: はず. Known fact, now explained: わけ.
